J states 'established time limits for each phase' unconditionally and omits the justify-and-document requirement.

explanation: G (211.111; 211.113) is the correct governing pair. J is accurate as far as it goes but drops the 'when appropriate' condition and the requirement that deviations be justified and documented (211.111), and reduces 211.113(b) to sterilization validation, omitting aseptic process validation. These are affirmative requirements in the cited text, so the key is substantially right but incomplete.

question_interpretation: For an OOS HPLC assay result, asks what Part 211 requires (binding) and what the Barr Laboratories decision (US v. Barr Labs, D.N.J. 1993) and the FDA OOS framework add (case law and nonbinding guidance).

issues.detail: J lists 'Phase I laboratory investigation and Phase II full-scale investigation; no invalidation without assignable cause' alongside the 211.192 elements with no indication that they come from FDA's nonbinding OOS guidance (Revision 1, May 2022) and a 1993 district-court opinion, not from Part 211. The question asks for exactly this split, so the key should label the source of each element.

The 'Phase I / Phase II' terminology is FDA guidance terminology (guidance sections III and IV); the guidance cites the Barr opinion only for the point that outlier testing should not be used to invalidate chemical assays. Calling Phase I/II the 'Barr decision framework' is a common industry shorthand, not something the guidance or Part 211 states. Whether the opinion itself used a two-phase structure could not be checked against the opinion text.

J omits the guidance/Barr limits on testing into compliance: retests must be predefined in an SOP with a set maximum number, resampling only under predetermined procedures, no averaging that hides an OOS individual result, and no outlier tests to invalidate chemical assays. It also omits related binding provisions the guidance relies on: 211.165(f) (reject batches failing specifications), 211.194 (complete data from all tests kept), and 211.160(a) (deviations recorded and justified).

explanation: 211.192 is correctly identified as the binding source of the investigation duty (thorough investigation, extension to other batches and products, written record with conclusions and follow-up), and 211.160(b) is a reasonable second citation. The answer elements labelled as the 'Barr framework' are substantively consistent with FDA's OOS guidance (Phase I lab investigation; Phase II full-scale; invalidation only with a documented test event that caused the result), but J does not mark them as nonbinding guidance or case law. It also omits the retest, averaging and outlier limits that are the core of what Barr added. A court decision and guidance are not regulations, and a model that presented the phases as Part 211 requirements would score full marks under this key.
proposed_corrected_answer: Binding (Part 211): an OOS result must be thoroughly investigated whether or not the batch is distributed; the investigation extends to other batches and products that may be associated; and a written record with conclusions and follow-up is required (211.192). Laboratory controls must be scientifically sound (211.160(b)) and deviations recorded and justified (211.160(a)). Batches failing specifications must be rejected (211.165(f)), and complete data from all tests must be retained (211.194). Nonbinding (FDA OOS guidance, Rev. 1, May 2022, drawing on United States v. Barr Laboratories, D.N.J. 1993): Phase I laboratory investigation (analyst/supervisor assessment of data accuracy); if no laboratory error is found, a Phase II full-scale investigation (production review plus additional lab testing under predefined procedures). A result may be invalidated only on the observation and documentation of a test event that can reasonably be determined to have caused the OOS result. No 'testing into compliance': the maximum number of retests is specified in advance in an SOP, averaging must not hide an OOS individual result, and outlier tests should not be used to invalidate chemical assays (Barr). A confirmed OOS result leads to rejection and a batch-failure investigation extended to other batches.

question_interpretation: Asks for the general records and reports requirements of 21 CFR 211.180 (retention, availability, form of records, annual review, management notification).

issues.detail: Retention is at least 1 year after the batch expiration date, but for OTC products exempt from expiration dating under 211.137 it is 3 years after distribution (211.180(a),(b)). J gives only the 1-year rule. Component, container, closure and labeling records follow the same rule keyed to the last lot (211.180(b)).

J omits 211.180(d) (originals or true copies; reader/copy equipment) and 211.180(f) (procedures to notify responsible officials in writing of investigations under 211.198/204/208, recalls, FDA inspectional observations and regulatory actions). It also omits the required content of the annual evaluation procedures (representative batches; complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged products, 211.192 investigations) (211.180(e)(1),(2)). 'Record system' is vague and not a term the regulation uses.

explanation: 211.180 is the correct section and the J elements are broadly supported: 1-year post-expiration retention, records readily available for inspection (211.180(c)), and at-least-annual product quality evaluation (211.180(e)). But J omits the 3-year alternative for expiry-exempt OTC products and the management-notification requirement of 211.180(f), both material parts of the general requirements.
proposed_corrected_answer: Batch-associated production, control and distribution records are kept at least 1 year after batch expiration (3 years after distribution for expiry-exempt OTC products) (a). Component, container, closure and labeling records follow the same rule, keyed to the last lot using them (b). All records are readily available for authorized inspection at the establishment during retention; electronic retrieval from another location is acceptable (c). Originals or true copies are permitted (d). QCU review is required for complaints 'involving the possible failure of a drug product to meet any of its specifications', with a determination of whether a 211.192 investigation is needed. J states QCU review without that scope.

J says only 'record contents and retention'. Retention is at least 1 year after the drug product's expiration date or 1 year after the complaint was received, whichever is longer; for expiry-exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution (211.198(b)). Required content is the product name and strength, lot number, complainant name, nature of complaint and reply, plus investigation findings and follow-up, or the reason no investigation was needed and who decided (211.198(b)(1)-(3)). The file location rule is also omitted.

explanation: 211.198 is the correct section, but J misstates the adverse-experience cross-reference: the regulation names 310.305 and 514.80, not Part 314. That is a demonstrable citation error inside the answer key. A model answer that correctly quotes '310.305 and 514.80' would not match J's 'Part 310 or 314'. J also leaves the retention period and record contents unspecified and drops the condition on QCU review.
proposed_corrected_answer: Written procedures for handling all written and oral complaints, established and followed, including: QCU review of any complaint involving possible failure to meet specifications and a determination of whether a 211.192 investigation is needed; and review of whether the complaint is a serious and unexpected adverse drug experience reportable under 21 CFR 310.305 (and 514.80 for animal drugs) (211.198(a)). A written record of each complaint is kept in a designated complaint file at the manufacturing/processing/packing establishment, or elsewhere if readily available for inspection. Records are kept at least 1 year after the product's expiration date or 1 year after receipt of the complaint, whichever is longer, or 3 years after distribution for expiry-exempt OTC products. question_interpretation: Asks for the Part 211 Subpart K requirements for returned drug products (211.204) and drug product salvaging (211.208).

issues.detail: Destruction under 211.204 is required only where the holding, storage or shipping conditions, or the condition of the product or its container, carton or labeling, cast doubt on its safety, identity, strength, quality or purity. Even then destruction is avoided if examination, testing or other investigations prove the product meets standards. J ('destruction unless testing supports suitability') drops the triggering condition, and 211.204 also permits reprocessing.

J omits for returned products: required records (name and label potency, lot number, reason for return, quantity, date and ultimate disposition); a 211.192 investigation when the reason for return implicates associated batches; and written, followed procedures for holding, testing and reprocessing. For salvage: products subjected to improper storage conditions from disasters, fires, accidents or equipment failures must not be salvaged. Where that is in question, salvage needs BOTH laboratory evidence of meeting standards AND premises-inspection evidence, and organoleptic exams are only supplemental.

explanation: 211.204 and 211.208 are the correct sections and J is broadly consistent with them. But J overstates the destruction rule by dropping its 'casts doubt' trigger, omits reprocessing, return records, associated-batch investigation and written procedures, and reduces 211.208's two-part evidentiary test to 'specified conditions'.
proposed_corrected_answer: Returned products (211.204): identify as returned and hold. If holding, storage or shipping conditions, or the product, container, carton or labeling condition, cast doubt on safety, identity, strength, quality or purity, destroy the product unless examination, testing or other investigations prove it meets appropriate standards; reprocessing is allowed if the resulting product meets standards. Records must cover name and label potency, lot number, reason for return, quantity, disposition date and ultimate disposition. A 211.192 investigation is required if the reason for return implicates associated batches. Written procedures for holding, testing and reprocessing must be followed. Salvage (211.208): products subjected to improper storage conditions (temperature, humidity, smoke, fumes, pressure, age, radiation) from natural disasters, fires, accidents or equipment failures must not be salvaged and returned to market. Where that is in question, salvage is allowed only with (a) laboratory evidence that standards are met and (b) premises-inspection evidence that the products and packaging were not exposed. Organoleptic examination is supplemental only. Records of name, lot number and disposition must be kept.
